meta.description: No evidence Ernest Hemingway wrote this six-word story. The motif circulated from 1906–1921; the Hemingway legend dates only to a 1989 play.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'For sale: baby shoes, never worn'?
meta.ogDescription: Hemingway almost certainly didn't write it. The 'baby shoes' story predates his fame and was pinned to his name only in 1989.

answer.label: Not Ernest Hemingway — an unfounded literary legend
answer.authorDates: Story motif documented from 1906; credited to Hemingway only since 1989
answer.sourceLine: There is no documented source in which Hemingway wrote or spoke this line — no manuscript, letter, interview, or contemporary account. Quote Investigator ↗ found the ‘baby shoes / never used’ idea circulating in classified ads and writing manuals years before Hemingway was famous, and the story was tied to him only in 1989 — 28 years after his death.

source.heading: Where the legend really comes from

docMeta.dd: Anonymous; ‘baby shoes / never used’ motif in print by 1906–1921
Papa: A Play Based on the Legendary Lives of Ernest Hemingway

source.excerpt: For sale: baby shoes, never worn.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive evidence that Ernest Hemingway composed this six word story,” tracing ‘baby shoes / never used’ ad-and-story motifs back to the early 1900s.

A 1917 essay by editor William R. Kane in The Editor proposed “Little Shoes, Never Worn” as a story title, and in 1921 columnist Roy K. Moulton printed a version crediting a ‘Jerry’ — per Wikipedia’s survey ↗.
The Hemingway attribution first appears in John de Groot’s 1989 one-man play Papa and a 1991 book by literary agent Peter Miller, who claimed he heard it around 1974 — Wikipedia ↗.
source.excerptNote: The popular anecdote — Hemingway betting fellow writers $10 each that he could write a story in six words, then scrawling this on a napkin — is itself undocumented and first appears in John de Groot’s 1989 play.
source.rightsNote: The exact six-word wording has no identifiable author or first publication — it crystallized out of decades of anonymous classified-ad and writing-manual variants — so no copyright status can honestly be asserted. It is not a documented Hemingway text.

author.name: Ernest Hemingway
author.heading: Why it gets blamed on Hemingway
author.bio: Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961) won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954 and is celebrated for a spare, economical style — which is exactly why a devastating six-word story feels like his. But no letter, manuscript, interview, or contemporary account records him writing it, and the anecdote surfaced only decades after his death. He is the credited name, not the documented author.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared ‘Hemingway’ lines on the internet — and one of the least likely to be his.

items.why: No manuscript, letter, or contemporary account has him writing this. Quote Investigator ↗ notes versions circulated when Hemingway was a child, and he was first credited only in 1989.
The dramatic bet story is undocumented and first appears in a 1989 play; the venue, stakes, and witnesses vary wildly between tellings — a hallmark of folklore, per Wikipedia ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The ‘baby shoes’ motif is genuine folk literature with roots as far back as 1906 — but crediting the six-word story to Hemingway is a late-20th-century myth, not literary history (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why it stuck
lead: The line endures because it works: six words that imply an entire tragedy, attached to a famous name known for saying much with little. That fit is precisely why the misattribution spread so far — it feels like Hemingway, even though the story elements were circulating in classified ads and writing manuals before he published a word.
context.pull: Six words that imply a whole tragedy — but not, on any evidence, Hemingway’s six words.
